paras: The lynching of Lamb Whitely was the killing of a Black man by a mob on the Smithland plantation near Monterey Landing, Concordia Parish, Louisiana, reported from Jonesville on June 26, 1903. According to the dispatch, Whitely was accused of assaulting a white man, and the mob took him to the woods and "riddled his body with bullets." The brief wire report ran in white papers across the country and in the Baltimore Afro-American, and the case was entered in monthly and year-end lists of lynchings, but no follow-up report was found.

The Smithland plantation was in Concordia Parish; one version of the dispatch placed it ten miles from Monterey Landing, others simply "near" the landing, and one paper printed the name as "Montgomery Landing." The news came to Jonesville, Louisiana, and a special correspondent of the Memphis Commercial-Appeal sent it from there to Memphis, which put it on the wire under a June 26 date. Papers spelled the surname as Whitely, Whitley, Whittle, Whitly, Whitney and White, but all gave the first name as Lamb and described him as "a negro" or "colored."

The dispatch gave the cause in one clause, "Whitely assaulted a white man," stating the accusation as fact without naming the man. A mob then took Whitely to the woods and shot him, the report said, leaving his body "riddled" with bullets. No report gave the size of the mob, named its members, mentioned officers, or said whether Whitely had been arrested.

No report of an inquest, arrest, or prosecution appears in the coverage, and the white man said to have been assaulted is not named in any report. The case returned instead in tallies: a Plymouth, Indiana, paper noted that it was "the nineteenth lynching in the United States during June," and July lists of the month's lynchings entered "Lamb Whitely, colored, Monterey Landing, La." Year-end chronologies printed through February 1904, including one in the St. Tammany Farmer of Covington, Louisiana, listed him under June 26 with the offense given as "murder."

The short wire item appeared first in papers of June 27, 1903, from Birmingham and Washington to Salt Lake City. The Washington Times headed it "Lynching in Louisiana" and the Deseret Evening News "Louisiana Negro Lynched." Others were flippant: the St. Paul Globe ran "Pelicans Do Some Lynching," and the Bemidji Daily Pioneer "Negro Gets It in the Neck." Digest columns cut the story to a single sentence, as in the Alexandria Gazette's "News of the Day" and the Semi-Weekly Interior Journal of Stanford, Kentucky, while weeklies reprinted the full text into early July.

The only editorial comment found came from the Burlington Weekly Free Press, which cited the case to argue that in the South the offenses for which men were lynched were becoming "less serious." The Free Press observed that the dispatch did not say what provocation the white man had given or that the assault was serious. Its summary was blunt: "The negro struck a white man or was charged with striking one; so he was taken into the woods and lynched."

In the Black press, the Baltimore Afro-American reprinted the wire text on July 4 under the headline "Negro Lynched in Louisiana," without comment and among unrelated news items. On January 2, 1904, the Chicago Broad Ax listed the case under June 26 in the same year-end chronology of lynchings that white papers such as the Waterbury Evening Democrat printed; its entry breaks off after "near Monte-."

Versions differed on the accusation. Most said Whitely had "assaulted a white man," while the St. Paul Globe and the Bemidji Daily Pioneer said he had assaulted a white woman. A Watertown, Wisconsin, digest said he was killed "for murdering a white man," and the year-end chronologies gave the offense as "murder." The earliest and most widely printed text said a white man, and none of the variants cites a separate source.

The date is also uncertain: the dispatch of June 26 said only that the news had reached Jonesville, and the Alexandria Gazette's digest placed the killing "yesterday." The July lists of June lynchings dated it June 25, while the year-end chronologies gave June 26.

reader.title: Lynching of Lamb Whitely
bases: A mob took a Black man accused of assaulting a white man into the woods and shot him to death (A1, A2, A6).

Every report says a 'mob' took Whitely to the woods and riddled his body with bullets (A1, A2, A6), with no lawful authority mentioned; the stated reason was punishment for an alleged assault on a white man (A1), and later lists counted it as a lynching (A21, A26).

All contemporary reports trace to one Commercial-Appeal special from Jonesville (A1, A4, A6), and the lists and the Afro-American copy repeat it (A19, A21, A26); no independent local account was found.

The Burlington Weekly Free Press cited it as lynching for an offense not shown to be serious.
The Baltimore Afro-American ran the wire text as 'Negro Lynched in Louisiana' without comment; the Chicago Broad Ax carried it in a syndicated year chronology.
